events.title: March-May 2022 attack wave in Israel and Operation Break the Wave
events.title_he: גל הפיגועים במרץ-מאי 2022 ומבצע שוברים גלים
events.summary: Between late March and May 2022 a series of attacks killed Israelis in Beersheba (four killed), Hadera (two Border Police officers killed), Bnei Brak (five killed), Tel Aviv (three killed in April) and Elad (four killed). Israeli authorities, as reported by the US State Department, counted 21 Israelis killed from March to May; the attackers included Arab citizens of Israel, whom the authorities described in one case as inspired by ISIS, and Palestinians from the West Bank. Prime Minister Bennett described the attacks as a wave of terrorism, and the IDF launched Operation Break the Wave, with almost daily raids in the West Bank for the rest of the year. According to figures the UN gave the Washington Post, Israeli security forces killed 146 Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 2022 through 19 December, against 75 in 2021; that figure covers the whole year and is not broken down for March to May.

affected_populations.note: US State Dept report (citing Israeli authorities): 21 Israelis killed by terrorist attacks, March to May 2022. Listed attacks: Beersheba 4, Hadera 2 (Border Police), Bnei Brak 5, Tel Aviv 3, Elad 4.

events.title: Journalist Shireen Abu Akleh killed in Jenin
events.title_he: הריגתה של העיתונאית שירין אבו עאקלה
events.summary: On 11 May 2022 Al Jazeera correspondent Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American, was shot dead while covering an Israeli arrest operation in the Jenin refugee camp; her producer Ali Samoudi was wounded. On 24 June 2022 the UN human rights office said its monitoring was consistent with the shots having come from Israeli Security Forces and that Israel had not opened a criminal investigation; the Israeli mission in Geneva rejected that conclusion, citing the Palestinian Authority's refusal to hand over the bullet. On 5 September 2022 the IDF concluded it was not possible to determine the source of the fire unequivocally but that there was a high possibility she was accidentally hit by IDF gunfire aimed at armed Palestinians. Her family rejected the findings and called for an independent US investigation.

events.title: Operation Breaking Dawn: Israel-Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighting in Gaza
events.summary: On 5 August 2022 Israel struck Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) targets in Gaza, killing its northern Gaza commander Tayseer Jabari, in what Israel said was a pre-emptive operation against an imminent attack; Khaled Mansour was killed in Rafah on 7 August. PIJ and other groups fired roughly 1,100 rockets and projectiles at Israel, about 200 of which fell short inside Gaza according to Israeli sources. A ceasefire brokered by Egypt and the UN took effect at 23:30 on 7 August. The UN human rights office confirmed 48 Palestinians killed including 17 children; OCHA's earlier verified count was 46; the Gaza health ministry figure reported by the Israeli Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center was 44. Israel and Palestinian sources dispute who caused some deaths: the Israeli army says an explosion in Jabalia that killed six people, including four children, was caused by a misfired Palestinian rocket, while Palestinian sources attribute it to an Israeli airstrike. Magen David Adom took 47 Israelis to hospital (Israeli authorities reported 70 injured); the US State Department reported no Israeli casualties from the rocket fire.

affected_populations.note: OHCHR 48 killed incl. 17 children (11 Aug 2022); OCHA verified 46 incl. 15 children as of 8 Aug; Gaza health ministry as reported by ITIC: 44 killed, 360 wounded. Israel says some deaths, especially of children, were caused by Palestinian rocket misfires; Palestinian sources attribute them to Israeli strikes. Includes PIJ members (Jerusalem Brigades said 12 operatives killed, per ITIC).

Magen David Adom evacuated 47 to hospital; Israeli authorities reported 70 injured (OCHA). US State Dept reports no Israeli casualties from rocket fire (intercepted or fell in open areas); the breakdown of the injuries is not given in the sources.

events.title: Deferral of army service for yeshiva students agreed (about 400 students)
events.summary: In 1948 Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion approved a request from Agudat Yisrael to exempt about 400 full-time yeshiva students from military service, following a pre-state order by Haganah chief of staff Yisrael Galili not to conscript yeshiva students on approved lists. It was justified at the time by the need to restore the Torah world destroyed in the Holocaust, and Ben-Gurion believed the number would diminish. The arrangement began as a quota of roughly 400 deferrals a year and was later widened by administrative decisions (Shimon Peres and yeshiva heads in 1958, an 800-per-year cap after 1967, and the removal of limits by the Begin government in 1977). In a 1958 reply to Rabbi Herzog, who defended yeshiva students as also being enlisted in safeguarding Israel's religion and heritage, Ben-Gurion argued it was first of all a moral issue whether one mother's son should be killed defending the homeland while another studies in safety.

cite.claim: Pre-state order not to conscript yeshiva students on approved lists
cite.quote: 1948 (pre-state) – Yisrael Galili, Chief of Staff of the Haganah, ordered not to conscript yeshiva students included in the "approve lists" to IDF brigades.

cite.claim: Ben-Gurion approved exempting 400 yeshiva students at Agudat Yisrael's request
cite.quote: 1948 – Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion approved the decision, and complied with Agudat Yisrael's request to exempt 400 yeshiva students from military service.

cite.claim: Only about 400 such students; Ben-Gurion expected the number to shrink
cite.quote: There were only 400 such young men at the time, and Ben-Gurion believed the number would diminish.
At that time, in 1948, it was justified by the need to restore the Torah world that was destroyed in the Holocaust.

cite.claim: Initial quota of about 400 a year
cite.quote: Initially there was a fixed quota of Yeshiva students whose service was deferred, not exceeding about four hundred (400) Yeshiva students a year.
1958 – Shimon Peres, then-Director General of the Ministry of Defense, together with the heads of the yeshivas, signs an arrangement to continue the exemption, subject to active yeshiva studies.

1967 – After the Six-Day War, in light of the gradual increase in the number of draft exemptions, the Minister of Defense determined as part of the arrangement that each year there would be 800 yeshiva students eligible for exemption.
1977 – The Begin government lifted the restrictions on the number of yeshivas whose students are entitled or eligible for exemptions.
Rabbi Herzog wrote to Ben-Gurion of his concern, claiming that "they, too [the yeshiva students], are enlisted and safeguard Israel's religion and heritage

This is, first and foremost, a great moral issue: whether it is fitting that the son of one mother is killed in defence of the homeland, and another mother's son sits in his room and studies in safety

events.title: Knesset passes the Tal Law on yeshiva-student deferrals
events.summary: On 23 July 2002 the Knesset voted 51-41 to approve the Tal Law, an effort to address the growing problem of Haredi men receiving exemptions from military service. The law followed a 1998 High Court ruling that the defence minister lacked the authority to grant sweeping exemptions to yeshiva students without explicit legislation, and the Tal Committee formed under Ehud Barak in 1999. For the first time it regulated the deferral of yeshiva students' service in law. In 2006 a nine-judge High Court panel declined to invalidate it despite its disproportionate impact on equality. Supporters of the exemption argue Torah study protects the state; critics, including the petitioners who challenged the law, argue it undermines equality in the burden of service.

cite.quote: July 23, 2002 The Knesset votes 51-41 to approve the Tal Law, an effort to address the growing problem of Haredi Jews receiving exemptions from military service.

cite.claim: Based on the Tal Committee formed in 1999

cite.quote: the Minister of Defense does not have the authority to grant a sweeping exemption from military service to large numbers of yeshiva students without explicit authorization by law.

events.title: High Court strikes down the Tal Law
events.summary: On 21 February 2012 the High Court of Justice struck down the Tal Law by a 6-3 vote, ruling that it could not be renewed. The majority opinion, written by outgoing court President Dorit Beinisch, found the state had failed to show that the law was achieving its goal of raising Haredi enlistment and reducing discrimination in the draft; because yeshiva students are often already raising families by 22, the deferral effectively acted as an exemption. The Israel Democracy Institute summarises the reasoning as insufficiently robust equality in burden-sharing mechanisms. A Jewish Week editorial at the time put the number of exempted yeshiva students at about 70,000, against 400 in 1948. Defence Minister Ehud Barak welcomed the decision.

events.title: High Court rules the state must draft yeshiva students
events.summary: On 25 June 2024 a nine-judge High Court panel ruled unanimously that Israel must draft Haredi men into the army and cannot keep funding yeshivas whose students enrol in lieu of service. The blanket exemption law had expired the previous year and the government had decided to keep not conscripting yeshiva students. The petition was filed by the Movement for Quality Government in Israel, which called the ruling a new page in the state's history. Haredi leaders contend that Torah study has inherent value and protects the state; United Torah Judaism's Moshe Gafni said there had never been a Supreme Court ruling in favour of yeshiva members, and one Haredi leader warned of 'two states'. Haredi parties in Netanyahu's coalition are irrevocably opposed to mandating Haredi conscription, and the judges referred to gradual conscription.

cite.quote: Israel must draft haredi Orthodox Jews into its army, the country’s Supreme Court ruled in a unanimous decision Tuesday.
By Philissa Cramer June 25, 2024 9:20 am
Now, nine judges on Israel’s High Court have ruled that the government must begin conscripting haredi men — and also cannot continuing funding yeshivas that enroll haredi men in lieu of army service.
When the latest blanket exemption law expired last year, Israel’s right-wing government decided to continue not conscripting yeshiva students

“Today a new page was written in the history of the State of Israel,” the Movement for Quality Government in Israel, a nonprofit that has spearheaded public advocacy on the issue for decades and filed the petition in the latest case, said in its statement .
Haredi leaders contend that Torah study has inherent value and serves to protect the state, and that accommodating the religious needs of haredi men would itself be a burden for the army.
“There has never been a ruling by the Supreme Court in favor of the members of the yeshiva and in the interest of the haredi public,” tweeted Moshe Gafni of United Torah Judaism.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, which includes haredi parties that are irrevocably opposed to mandating haredi conscription.
the judges referred to “gradual conscription of yeshiva students.”

events.title: Mughrabi Quarter of the Old City demolished and residents evicted
events.summary: On 10 June 1967, days after Israeli forces took the Old City, the Mughrabi (Moroccan) Quarter beside the Western Wall in Jerusalem was cleared and demolished to create the Western Wall plaza. Sources give the number evicted as approximately 650 people (Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs) or 108 families (Israel Hayom); MERIP says more than 100 families were told they had three hours to leave. Mayor Teddy Kollek and army officers gave the order, according to the JCPA; Kollek later wrote that something had to be done about the small slum houses crowding the Wall. The JCPA argues the demolition was justified and necessary for public safety and for tens of thousands of worshippers expected at Shavuot, and says many residents later received compensation; it describes the New Yorker article it answers as calling the demolition a war crime under the Fourth Geneva Convention. French historian Vincent Lemire cites minutes of a 9 June meeting between Kollek and the army commander listing the quarter's destruction as an agenda item, and argues it was premeditated and planned.

displacement.note: JCPA: approximately 650 Arab inhabitants; Israel Hayom: 108 families; MERIP: more than 100 families

affected_populations.note: JCPA: approximately 650 residents evicted; Israel Hayom: 108 families; MERIP: more than 100 families. No deaths are reported in the cited sources; none were counted either way.

cite.claim: Work completed overnight; 108 families removed (Israel Hayom)
cite.quote: Overnight, on June 10, 1967, the work was completed. The 108 families who had lived in the Mughrabi Quarter were removed.

The only answer was to do away with the slum hovels of the Moghrabi Quarter

From a legal standpoint, the demolition of the Mughrabi Quarter and relocation of its inhabitants was justified and necessary by any acceptable standard to ensure public safety and security and to provide tens of thousands of worshippers with a safe, sanitary passage to Judaism’s most holy site, and sufficient public space to worship there.

events.title: Jewish Quarter of the Old City surrenders to the Arab Legion
events.summary: On 28 May 1948 the besieged defenders of the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City surrendered to Jordan's Arab Legion; a Truce Commission telegram put the unconditional surrender at 6 p.m. Israel National News says the remaining 1,600 residents were gathered in Batei Machseh Square, about 1,300 women, children and elderly were evacuated to Jewish-held Jerusalem and close to 300 males were taken prisoner; the US vice consul's telegram of 29 May recorded surrender terms of about 2,000 evacuees under Red Cross supervision and 300 men of military age taken prisoner. A UN representative present told the US consulate the Arab Legion had carried out the evacuation efficiently and according to the agreement, while a Jewish Agency official said Arab irregulars on the walls fired on the armoured buses carrying evacuees.

events.title: Battles of Latrun: Israeli attacks on the Arab Legion fort fail
events.summary: After the British withdrew in mid-May 1948, Jordan's Arab Legion took the Latrun fort that overlooks the road from the coastal plain to Jerusalem; Israeli sources describe this as strengthening a siege of Jerusalem's roughly 100,000 Jews. Israeli accounts say Ben-Gurion regarded capturing Latrun as the key to liberating Jerusalem. The first assault (Operation Bin Nun Alef, 24-25 May) and a second on 1 June (Bin Nun Bet) failed with heavy Israeli losses, including recent immigrants and Holocaust survivors who had arrived days earlier; three later attacks also failed. The Jewish Virtual Library gives an official Israeli casualty figure of 139 for both main battles, while another source puts the first attack alone at about 75 killed. Israel instead opened the Burma Road bypass, whose first convoy left on 1 June and which could take full-size trucks by 10 June. Latrun stayed in Jordanian hands until the Six-Day War in June 1967.

affected_populations.note: Low: about 75 killed in the first attack (CIE); high: official figure of 139 for both main battles (JVL). Sources differ.

events.title: Lausanne Conference of the UN Conciliation Commission (Israel and the Arab states)
events.summary: From 27 April 1949 the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine met separate Israeli and Arab delegations in Lausanne. On 12 May 1949 it obtained from Israel and the Arab delegations (separately but identically) a Protocol taking a map of the 1947 partition plan as a basis for discussion; the Arabs claimed this amounted to Israeli recognition of the Partition Plan, while Israel held the map was 'a, and not the, basis' for negotiations. The Arab delegations insisted that Israel first accept the principle of repatriation of refugees set out in General Assembly resolution 194, and proposed the immediate return of refugees from territories under Israeli authority that formed part of the Arab zone on the map; Israel said it would accept as citizens the whole Arab population of the Gaza area, including refugees, if Gaza were incorporated into Israel, but declined to propose refugee numbers otherwise. The Commission's 12 September meeting with the Israeli delegation was the last before it adjourned, and UNISPAL summarises it as a lack of progress on the refugee and territorial issues.

events.title: Duma arson attack kills three members of a Palestinian family
events.summary: In the early hours of 31 July 2015 attackers firebombed a house in the West Bank village of Duma, near Nablus, killing 18-month-old Ali Dawabsheh; his parents Saad and Riham also died, and his four-year-old brother Ahmad survived with severe burns. Graffiti on the walls included the word 'revenge'. Prime Minister Netanyahu called the attack an act of terrorism in every respect, while the PLO held the Israeli government responsible, saying it was a direct consequence of decades of impunity given to settler terrorism. In May 2020 the Lod District Court gave Amiram Ben-Uliel a triple conviction, and in September 2020 sentenced him to three consecutive life terms plus 20 years; the Shin Bet called the verdict an important milestone in the struggle against Jewish terrorism, while Ben-Uliel said investigators had forced a false confession from him.

events.title: Stabbing attack at the Jerusalem Pride parade; Shira Banki dies
events.summary: On the evening of Thursday 30 July 2015 an ultra-Orthodox Jewish man, Yishai Schlissel, stabbed six people at the Jerusalem Pride parade; two were seriously hurt. He had been released from prison about three weeks earlier after serving a sentence for stabbing several people at the 2005 parade, and was arrested at the scene. Sixteen-year-old Shira Banki died of her wounds on Sunday 2 August 2015. In 2016 Schlissel, who had refused legal counsel and said the court did not recognise Jewish law, was convicted of murder and six counts of attempted murder, and sentenced to life in prison.

affected_populations.note: Six marchers were stabbed, among them Shira Banki, 16, who died on 2 August 2015; two were seriously hurt on the night. The attacker is an ultra-Orthodox Israeli Jew.
